title: Shine Targets and Assignments
subtitle: One zone is clean, but the rest of the home is still unnamed, and Shine that belongs to no one lands on the same tired pair of hands. This chapter lists every target worth cleaning, groups it so nothing hides, and puts a name against each one, so the whole home gets read and the work gets shared.

It teaches the reader to see cleaning targets by kind (four categories, home-scaled from the source: surfaces, equipment and fixtures, stored things, point of use), builds one Shine list that drags the invisible targets into view, and puts a name against every line so the work is shared instead of silently absorbed by one person. Chapter 18 (Cleaning Methods That Actually Work) gives each target on the list its how, the quick, effective methods that make cleaning fast enough to actually happen.
audience: Readers who have finished Chapter 16, reframed cleaning as inspection, and made one first cleaning-and-inspection pass on the launch pad, and who now face the rest of the home: still unread, still unnamed, and in most households quietly falling to one person. Busy home keepers and parents. Applying the method, not new to it. They do not need to re-argue why we clean or to re-sort or re-arrange; they need a plan that covers the whole home (what needs cleaning, grouped so nothing hides) and a fair way to share it (a name on every target), so Shine survives contact with a real household instead of collapsing back onto the usual person.
core_promise: Turn one first cleaning pass into a whole-home plan and share the labor. Learn to see cleaning targets by KIND rather than by room (the four categories, home-scaled: surfaces, equipment and fixtures, stored things, point of use), build one Shine list that surfaces the invisible targets (the tops, backs, undersides, insides, and handles), and put a NAME against every line so the work is shared instead of silently dumped. Keep two rules: clean the whole thing, not just the part that shows; and a job that belongs to everyone belongs to no one, put a name on every target. Let people choose their targets rather than get handed them, matched to ability, with the worst jobs shared or rotated, all without re-sorting or re-arranging a single thing.
emotional_purpose: Deliver fairness and relief, not lecture. This chapter touches a live nerve, who does the housework, so the register is that the load falling on one person is a default to be fixed with a list and shared names, not a moral failing and not something to nag about. No shame: a home where the cleaning silently fell to one person is the common case, not a character flaw, and the fix is a list and shared names, not trying harder. The payoff is a home kept by everyone, which asks less of anyone and stops depending on one person never getting tired. Deliver the honest planning HOLD: naming and assigning is real, useful work, and it is not yet cleaning, so the needle holds where the first Shine step left it, with a dashed forward projection showing exactly where it is about to go once the plan is carried out.
practical_purpose: Show why cleaning the whole home needs a plan, not just more effort from one person (instinct cleans the same visible handful over and over and never touches the rest); teach the reader to see targets by the four kinds so the overlooked ones (especially stored things and point of use) come into view; build one whole-home Shine list grouped by kind, on a sheet of paper in about twenty minutes; teach the targets rule (clean the whole thing, not just the part that shows) and the invisible-target payoff (the surface that faces away is the one that fails); put a name against every line including the ones you would keep for yourself (the assignments rule); hand out the work by letting people choose rather than get handed, matched to ability, worst jobs shared or rotated; and read the friction meter as a principled HOLD (planning, not cleaning) with a dashed forward projection, the goal still ahead.

worked_example.space: The whole home, with the launch pad from Chapter 16 as its first entry. Instead of cleaning one more surface, the reader builds the Shine list: on a sheet of paper, the four kinds of target run down the page as headings, then a walk through the home, category by category, fills in the real targets under each and writes a name to the right of every line. The launch pad stops being a lucky exception and becomes line one on a list that now covers everything, owned by everyone.
worked_example.note: The four categories are not meant to be exhaustive or official; they give attention four different angles of approach, so the targets that hide from one angle get caught by another. The list is not re-sorting or re-arranging: when it touches stored things it means clean and check them, not decide again whether to keep them, which was done back in Sort. Nothing new is cleaned in this chapter; the reader makes the list and shares it.

target_categories.surfaces: The floors, walls, windows, counters, shelves, and doors, the flat faces of the home that show dirt and take the most traffic.
target_categories.equipment_and_fixtures: The appliances, the taps and sinks, the furniture, the tools, the working things that both get dirty and can quietly fail.
target_categories.stored_things: Whatever lives inside the cabinets, closets, drawers, and boxes, which need cleaning and checking too, even though a closed door hides them from view.
target_categories.point_of_use: The high-touch spots your hands hit a hundred times a day, the handles, the switches, the remotes, the pull on the launch pad drawer, the places that get the most human contact and almost none of the cleaning.

worked_example.assignments: Go down the list and assign every line, including the ones you would have silently kept for yourself, because a target with no name is a target quietly assigned back to the usual person. Make the list together and let people claim targets before anything gets assigned; match targets to who can actually do them (a child owns the light switches and low door handles, an adult takes the oven and the fridge coils); and share out or rotate the jobs nobody wants instead of letting them default back to one person.
worked_example.tally: Same room, same keepers, nothing cleaned that was not cleaned yesterday, but the invisible pile of obligation is now a finite, shareable set of lines, grouped so the hidden targets could not hide, with a name against each one so the work is shared instead of landing on a single pair of hands. The plan is real and shared even though nothing new was cleaned, so the friction meter holds where the first Shine step left it, with a dashed forward projection showing the move to come.

definition: A Shine list is one shared inventory of everything in a space that needs regular cleaning and inspection, grouped by kind of target, with a person's name against each one, so nothing is forgotten and no job quietly lands on a single pair of hands.
rule: Clean the whole thing, not just the part that shows.
support_line: A job that belongs to everyone belongs to no one. Put a name on every target.
one_idea_to_keep: List every target that needs cleaning, group it by kind so nothing hides, and put a name against each one. A Shine you have written down and shared is a Shine that actually happens, and it happens to the whole home, not just the parts that show and not just to the one person who always ends up doing it.

the trap of cleaning by instinct: it cleans what is in front of you and what is bothering you today, the same visible handful over and over, and never once touches the rest
see targets by KIND, not by room: a room-by-room sweep always misses the same things, and sorting the world into a few kinds of target drags the overlooked ones into the light

the four kinds of target, home-scaled from the source categories: surfaces (floors, walls, windows, counters, shelves, doors); equipment and fixtures (appliances, taps and sinks, furniture, tools); stored things (inside cabinets, closets, drawers, boxes, cleaned and checked, not re-sorted); point of use (handles, switches, remotes, the launch pad), the one people forget most

the hero device, the Shine list: one whole-home inventory grouped by kind with a name against each line, a sheet of paper and about twenty minutes, half its value done just by writing it down because you cannot share a feeling of obligation but you can share a list

do not aim for a perfect list on the first pass: a first Shine list is usually longer than people expect, not a verdict on how dirty the home is, just the first time it has all been written in one place instead of carried in one head

the targets rule, frozen: clean the whole thing, not just the part that shows, because the surface that faces the room is the one you clean and the surface that faces away is the one that fails (the microwave vent, the fridge coils, the sink overflow)

the invisible-target payoff, frozen: the dirt that matters is rarely the dirt you can see; it is on the top of the cupboard, behind the machine, under the mat, inside the drawer, and on the handle every hand in the house touches, and a target you never named is a surface no one ever reads

the assignments rule, frozen: a job that belongs to everyone belongs to no one, put a name on every target, because a list of targets with no names is just a longer, more detailed version of the guilt you started with

the no-owner default: the load falls on one person not by decision but by default, because an unassigned target flows to whoever notices first and cannot let it sit, the same person every time; nobody chose this, the absence of names chose it

the assignments reframe, frozen: a name against every target is not about control, it is about fairness, and about a home that stays cared for whether or not one person is watching; assign every line including the ones you would keep for yourself

choosing, not assigning, frozen: a job you chose is a job you will actually do, a job you were handed is a job you will resent; make the list together, let people pick before anyone gets handed the leftovers, match targets to ability (children own the low switches and handles), and share or rotate the worst jobs

the callback to Chapter 15's room map: a Shine list assigned together does to the cleaning what the room map did to the room, your room became their room; a home kept by everyone asks less of anyone and stops depending on one person never getting tired

the fences: do not re-argue why we clean beyond a one-line recap (Chapter 16), do not teach how to clean, products, or tools (Chapter 18), do not build the repeatable routine or reset (Chapter 19), and do not build documented standards or schedules (Standardize and Sustain); the Shine list is a target inventory plus owners, not a standard or a schedule; do not re-open Sort or Straighten
